# agent-browser core

Fast browser automation CLI for AI agents. Chrome/Chromium via CDP, no Playwright or Puppeteer dependency. Accessibility-tree snapshots with compact `@eN` refs let agents interact with pages in ~200-400 tokens instead of parsing raw HTML.

Most normal web tasks (navigate, read, click, fill, extract, screenshot) are covered here. Load a specialized skill when the task falls outside browser web pages — see [When to load another skill](#when-to-load-another-skill).

## The core loop

```bash
agent-browser open <url>        # 1. Open a page
agent-browser snapshot -i       # 2. See what's on it (interactive elements only)
agent-browser click @e3         # 3. Act on refs from the snapshot
agent-browser snapshot -i       # 4. Re-snapshot after any page change
```

Refs (`@e1`, `@e2`, ...) are assigned fresh on every snapshot. They become **stale the moment the page changes** — after clicks that navigate, form submits, dynamic re-renders, dialog opens. Always re-snapshot before your next ref interaction.

## Quickstart

```bash
# Install once
npm i -g agent-browser && agent-browser install

# Linux hosts can install required browser libraries too
agent-browser install --with-deps

# Take a screenshot of a page
agent-browser open https://example.com
agent-browser screenshot home.png
agent-browser close

# Search, click a result, and capture it
agent-browser open https://duckduckgo.com
agent-browser snapshot -i                      # find the search box ref
agent-browser fill @e1 "agent-browser cli"
agent-browser press Enter
agent-browser wait --load networkidle
agent-browser snapshot -i                      # refs now reflect results
agent-browser click @e5                        # click a result
agent-browser screenshot result.png
```

The browser stays running across commands so these feel like a single session. Use `agent-browser close` (or `close --all`) when you're done.

## MCP integration

For tools that support Model Context Protocol servers, start the stdio server:

```bash
agent-browser mcp
agent-browser mcp --tools all
agent-browser mcp --tools core,network,react
```

Configure the MCP client to launch `agent-browser` with `["mcp"]`. The server defaults to MCP protocol 2025-11-25 and accepts older supported client protocol versions during initialization. The default tools profile is `core`, which keeps MCP context small for everyday browser automation. Use `--tools all` for the full typed CLI parity surface, or combine profiles with commas, such as `--tools core,network,react`. Profiles are `core`, `network`, `state`, `debug`, `tabs`, `react`, `mobile`, and `all`; the `debug` profile includes plugin registry and command.run tools. Each tool accepts typed arguments plus `extraArgs` for advanced CLI flags and exact CLI parity. The common `allowedDomains` array maps to `--allowed-domains` and activates the same WebRTC containment and launch-mode restrictions. Tool discovery is paginated and includes read-only/open-world annotations so modern MCP clients can load the large typed surface incrementally. Use the tool `session` argument or `AGENT_BROWSER_SESSION` to isolate browser sessions.

## eve agent integration

For eve agents, mount the `@agent-browser/eve` extension instead of hand-writing browser tools. It adds namespaced tools such as `browser__navigate`, `browser__snapshot`, `browser__click`, `browser__fill`, `browser__find`, and `browser__screenshot`, all backed by agent-browser running inside the eve sandbox. The sandbox bootstrap helpers (`installAgentBrowser`, `agentBrowserRevalidationKey`) ship with the same package under `@agent-browser/eve/sandbox`, so `agent/sandbox.ts` needs no extra dependency.

## Reading a page

```bash
agent-browser snapshot                    # full tree (verbose)
agent-browser snapshot -i                 # interactive elements only (preferred)
agent-browser snapshot -i -u              # include href urls on links
agent-browser snapshot -i -c              # compact (no empty structural nodes)
agent-browser snapshot -i -d 3            # cap depth at 3 levels
agent-browser snapshot -s "#main"         # scope to a CSS selector
agent-browser snapshot -i --json          # machine-readable output
```

Snapshot output looks like:

```
Page: Example - Log in
URL: https://example.com/login

@e1 [heading] "Log in"
@e2 [form]
  @e3 [input type="email"] placeholder="Email"
  @e4 [input type="password"] placeholder="Password"
  @e5 [button type="submit"] "Continue"
  @e6 [link] "Forgot password?"
```

For unstructured reading (no refs needed):

```bash
agent-browser read                         # read rendered active-tab DOM
agent-browser read https://docs.example.com/guide  # docs-friendly fetch, prefers markdown
agent-browser read https://docs.example.com/guide --filter auth  # one matching section
agent-browser read https://docs.example.com/guide --outline  # compact page headings
agent-browser read https://docs.example.com --llms index --filter auth  # compact llms.txt discovery
agent-browser get text @e1                # visible text of an element
agent-browser get html @e1                # innerHTML
agent-browser get attr @e1 href           # any attribute
agent-browser get value @e1               # input value
agent-browser get title                   # page title
agent-browser get url                     # current URL
agent-browser get count ".item"           # count matching elements
```

Use `read [url]` when you need to consume documentation or other text pages rather than interact with a rendered UI. Omit the URL to read the rendered DOM of the active tab in the current browser session, including browser auth state and client-side updates. Explicit URL reads send `Accept: text/markdown`, try the same URL with `.md` appended when the first response is not markdown, walk ancestor paths toward `/` to find the nearest `llms.txt` for a matching docs link, print markdown/plain text when available, and fall back to readable text extracted from HTML without launching Chrome. Add `--filter <text>` to narrow a page to matching heading sections, `--outline` for compact headings on one page, `--llms index` for a compact nearest-ancestor `llms.txt` link list, and `--llms full` only when you explicitly need `llms-full.txt`. With `--llms` or `--require-md`, omitting the URL uses the active tab URL because those modes depend on HTTP resources. With `--llms` or `--outline`, `--filter <text>` narrows links, sections, or headings. Add `--require-md` when you specifically want to verify markdown negotiation, `--raw` when you need the response body unchanged, and `--json` when you need metadata such as `source` and `contentType`. Global safeguards such as `--allowed-domains`, `--content-boundaries`, and `--max-output` also apply to read fetches and output.

For sessions that handle sensitive data, use `--allowed-domains` to restrict navigations and page-initiated network traffic. Supported Chromium sessions also disable `RTCPeerConnection` while the allowlist is active so WebRTC STUN, TURN, and related DNS traffic cannot bypass the HTTP filter. Dedicated and shared workers are guarded with a bootstrap wrapper; if a page CSP forbids that wrapper, the worker fails closed rather than running without the allowlist guard. Pre-existing CDP sessions, auto-connect, Chrome profiles, direct-page provider plugins, agent-browser restore or state-file replay, raw Chrome args that select profiles, restore sessions, or open startup pages, iOS, and Safari reject this option because agent-browser cannot install equivalent containment before page scripts run. This is browser-level containment, not an operating-system firewall; see [Trust boundaries](references/trust-boundaries.md) for deployment guidance.

## Interacting

```bash
agent-browser click @e1                   # click
agent-browser click @e1 --new-tab         # open link in new tab instead of navigating
agent-browser dblclick @e1                # double-click
agent-browser hover @e1                   # hover

# Colophon

For the curious, and for my own memory, here's how this site came to be.

Process

## My Collaborator

I designed and built this site working with Claude Code, Anthropic’s agentic coding tool, as an experiment and a learning process. Designing a personal website is, in my experience, one of the hardest projects. The mix of blank-canvas freedom, deep personal investment, and the gap between ideas and execution tends to make them stall. Claude Code narrowed that gap in a way I hadn’t experienced before. I could stay focused on creative decisions rather than getting lost in implementation details. That’s new for me, and a little magical.

Because AI-assisted workflows are new to most of us, it feels worth describing how the collaboration actually went. As with any design project, I brought my own ideas about concept, color palette, typography, information hierarchy, and the overall user experience. I shared those with Claude Code, who in turn opened my eyes to ways I could extend them using technical solutions I wouldn’t have reached on my own. I’ve spent years teaching design, front-end, and server-side development, and I’ve built plenty of sites and apps, solo and with collaborators. This felt like old times sitting next to an engineer who helped bring my ideas to life and contributed her own. I never once felt like I was abdicating creativity. Quite the opposite. I felt more in touch with it.

I was occasionally in the code making my own tweaks, but I can’t hold a candle to what Claude can do there. I never opened a Figma file to figure out layout. I designed in the browser, which feels truer to the medium. Designing a picture of a website and then turning it into the real thing has always struck me as a silly way to do things. It tied my hands. I don’t think I’ll go back.

The Feels

## Design Influences

The visual language of the site draws from a few places. The stacked ridgeline plot in this header is not synthetic — it’s actual radio emission data from PSR B1919+21, the first radio pulsar ever discovered, recorded at 318 MHz by Harold Craft at Arecibo Observatory in 1970. Peter Saville used the same dataset for Joy Division’s Unknown Pleasures cover. The subtle animation reflects the pulsar’s actual 1.3373-second period.

The sounds of Hans Zimmer, Tangerine Dream, Boards of Canada, and Carbon Based Lifeforms were playing while I designed this site. No doubt this music influenced things.

Typography

## Typefaces

Display headings are set in F37 Lineca by F37 Foundry— a contemporary serif with an optical elegance that holds up at both large and small sizes. Its slightly negative sidebearing at display scale gives the headings their tight, confident stance.

Body copy, labels, and UI text are set in Aktiv Grotesk by Dalton Maag, served via Adobe Fonts. It pairs well with Lineca without competing.

Jedi knights vex Sith lords by quickly zapping the forgotten Wampa.F37 Lineca — Display

Joy quivers as love tears us apart; bleak fog hazes my dim, wrecked exit now.Aktiv Grotesk — Body

Audio Nerdery

## Sound Setup

Music matters to me, and dialing in the right listening experience is half the fun. After plenty of tinkering, here’s the setup that keeps me happy in the studio: a Thorens TD125 Mk II turntable, a McIntosh MA5100 integrated amp, and a pair of Klipsch Heresy IV speakers. Warm sound, beautiful objects. My kids will fight over this gear when I die.

Accessibility

## WCAG 2.1 AA

The site targets WCAG 2.1 Level AA compliance. A full audit was conducted covering landmark roles, heading structure, image alt text, keyboard navigation, focus management, color contrast, and motion preferences. All decorative canvas animations are hidden for users who have enabled prefers-reduced-motionin their OS settings. The lightbox, hamburger navigation, and contact form all have proper focus management so keyboard and screen reader users aren’t left stranded.

If you spot something that feels off, please file a bug.

Under the Hood

**Site 2 of 5: product.inc** (Alex Zapadenko, product designer)

What stands out:
1. **Seasonal theming.** The whole site is dressed for Halloween right now: castle, cape, pumpkins, orange accent. The banner reads "ships rough on purpose and gets better in public."

4. **Monogram that changes per section.** Top left reads "A — Z", then "T — A" as you scroll.
5. **One experiment is close to ours:** "Every token, component and screen in this site, drawn as one graph."
6. **Light/dark toggle**, a "Download resume" button, and a timeline résumé.

Their trade-off: a dense, long scroll that gets heavy.

**What do you like here?**

content.text:
**Site 3 of 5: gertix.studio** (German tech agency)

What stands out:
1. **Visible structure.** Dashed grid lines with "+" registration marks at the corners, like a print proof sheet. The scaffolding shows on purpose.
2. **Type pairing.** IBM Plex Mono for body and labels, ITC Avant Garde for headlines, all in uppercase, technical and editorial.
3. **Scroll-driven text fill.** Headlines go from grey to black as you scroll ("FÜNF DISZIPLINEN"). It's local, not the whole page.
4. **Pill keywords inside sentences.** Key terms sit in outlined pills in the middle of the copy.
5. **Stats row inside the grid**, with registration marks: 20+ years, 30+ partners, and so on.
6. **Stacked service panels.** Numbered (01, 02…) panels that change background color as they stack on scroll.
7. **Cinematic video hero**, plus a scrolling ticker of services at the bottom.

**What do you like here?**

content: We're in Phase 1, walking your 5 inspiration sites to shape the design brief, and site 3 of 5 (gertix.studio) is up. Next, tell me what you like or dislike about it, then we move to arturospatino.com.

message.content: This is another one that is just unique in some ways with subtle scroll effects. I like how they used the grid lines. It's perfectly themed/branded for their brand and what they offer. The pills for keywords was a nice way of "tagging" things while not looking like they're keyword cramming for SEO. I like the stacked service panels. I think what caught my eye was that and thinking about my pillars and having sections similar to this or follows the same idea(s). The cinematic video in the Hero is pretty cool. The footer has the two hands that react to the mouse hovering. Again, not saying I want to copy this site, but another good example of adding creative, clever branding for their company.

Maybe some graphics similar to this that aren't photos but represent whatever the theme of the jarodtaylor.com brand represents. **Site 5 of 5: eddy-naboulet.dev** (front-end and WebGL developer, France)

What stands out:
1. **The whole site is a fake retro operating system ("EDDY-OS").** It opens on a boot screen: "[ OK ] design memory … 15 years", "coffee.sys … running low", then "Press any key to enter".
2. **CRT look.** Amber-on-brown, pixel fonts (Jacquard 12, DotGothic16), curved screen corners, glow, and sound on by default.
3. **A desktop instead of pages.** A menu bar (File / Extras / System), live clock, "● available" status, and four "apps": projets.vol, parcours.log, profil.sys, contact.app.
4. **A waving ASCII-dither portrait** drawn in WebGL (three.js).
5. **The career shown as system data.** Years of design and engineering experience appear as boot-check lines.

Their trade-off: it's all one WebGL "screen". It's fun and memorable, but recruiters need to figure it out, and it's heavy. It's also the fake-terminal gimmick your IDEATION file warned against.

**What do you like here?** This is the last site. After this I'll sum up the patterns across all five.

# Thoughts, notes, open questions for jarodtaylor.com

**Companion file:** `CONTENT.md`

---

## Problem

Jarod has 18 years of strong, relevant work (design systems, frontend platforms, developer experience, engineering leadership) and almost none of it is public. His domain has said "coming soon" for years. Searching his name mostly shows other Jarod/Jared Taylors, including one he must never be confused with.

He needs one owned home on the web that:
1. tells a recruiter or hiring manager who he is in seconds,
2. proves his design engineering and frontend systems skill instead of just claiming it, and
3. gives him a place to publish writing that LinkedIn and X posts can link to.

## Audience

1. **Recruiters and hiring managers** (primary). Skimming. Need: role, seniority, proof, availability, contact.
2. **Engineering and design leaders / peers.** Reading posts. Need: substance, a reason to follow.
3. **Frontend and design engineers.** Will open dev tools and view source. Need: to be impressed by the craft.

## Positioning

> Designer turned engineer turned engineering leader. For 18 years I've built the work behind the work: design systems, frontend platforms, and developer experience that make whole engineering orgs faster. I've also led the teams that build them, through acquisitions, a bankruptcy, and more reorgs than I can count. These days I'm learning AI the way I learned everything else: hands-on, in public, with an ADHD brain running twenty threads at once.

**Four content pillars:** Leading engineering orgs · Design engineering and frontend systems · Developer experience · Learning AI in public.
**Honesty rule:** AI is framed as *learning in progress*, never as expertise. Don't add claims that aren't in `CONTENT.md`.

## Pages

Should this be a single page site? Homepage and Blog? Or best to have standard pages? If standard pages for growth reasons, initial thoughts:

* Homepage
* About
* Blog
* Work/Projects/Case Studies? A place where I can do case studies because as a leader at 3 different Fortune 500 I've delivered design systems and component libraries. This was done before the industry was even talking about design systems, tokens, etc. I also will have my personal projects/repos (mainly AI or Design System related) so I'm not sure if this belongs on the same page or something separate? 
* Is Contact Me even necessary anymore, or as part of the About Me (and in the footer) I have links to my Email, LinkedIn, Twitter/X, etc? 
* Colophon? This site will be like a portfolio piece, so why not have a page giving the details of how it was designed and built. Very similar to what this guy did: https://aarronwalter.com/colophon

## Ideas for the site

This is not exhaustive. Any new ideas we can come up with should be captured.

### Design System Driven

I'm an engineering leader with more than a decade of experience building Design Systems, Component Libraries, and Teams that build/curate them at Fortune 500 companies (enterprise companies). This site should demonstrate that. 

* **Tokens live in W3C Design Tokens (DTCG) JSON** in the repo, compiled to CSS. This is the source of truth that Figma Variables sync with. Brands should map cleanly to Figma Variable *modes*. Here are some Figma articles:

  * [Design token architecture: Structuring tokens for scale](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/design-token-architecture/)
  * [Design tokens: How to sync design and code in Figma](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/design-tokens/)
* **Design-system components are React (`.tsx`), rendered by Astro.** Pages and layouts stay `.astro`; reusable UI (buttons, tags, cards, nav, section shells, the Remix control) is React so standard `@storybook/react-vite` works with no community plugins.
  - Components render **server-side to static HTML by default** (no `client:*` directive). React ships to the browser only for islands that truly need it, so the zero-JS and Lighthouse targets still hold.
  - Component styles are **plain CSS, Tailwind, or CSS Modules) that consume tokens only**. No CSS-in-JS runtime, no hard-coded values. This keeps the "tokens, not framework" story honest.

* I want to show off the design system, tokens, and engineering side of my experience. So, the idea is one set of markup, completely restyled (not just themed colors, etc. but layout, component changes, spacing, typography, etc) all driven by the token system. A little modern take on the classic 2003 CSS Zen Garden which I actually learned from! My goal is to demonstrate the site from Figma -> Design Tokens (Style Dictionary, or another alternative) -> Storybook -> Website driven by the design system and tokens. We can always backfill Figma and Storybook once we've landed on the brand, design etc. on the website. 

* Initial goal would be at least **3 curated brands**: the default brand plus 2 alternates. They must differ in *more than color*: typography, type scale, spacing density, shape/radius, borders, and texture should all be able to change. 

* Maybe not v1 but I'd be curious if we could go beyond tokens and even toggle component configurations. For example, let's say we have a Hero on the page with text on the left, an eyebrow, paragraph and a graphic or image on the right. A component built correctly would allow a simple toggle to change the layout of that Hero. Again, this is just an idea, but could be something we explore AFTER v1 of the Remix system. 

* Tiered token architecture, visible in the source:

  - **Base/knob tier:** the few inputs a brand sets (e.g. base size, scale ratio, density, radius, border weight, fonts, palette).
  - **Semantic tier:** derived meanings (background, text, accent, spacing steps, type steps).
  - **Component tier:** what components consume.
  - Contrasting sections use **semantic surface roles** (e.g. `surface`, `surface-inverse`, `surface-accent`), never hard-coded colors. Each brand decides what each role looks like, and a future dark mode stays possible without a refactor.
  - A brand sets **only** the base tier. Everything else is derived. This is what makes Remix v2 (live knobs) possible later, so design for it now.
  - While remixing, the visitor can see *what changed*: which tokens changed and that zero markup did (e.g. "14 tokens changed · 0 lines of markup changed").
  - Switching brands transitions smoothly and respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
  - All brands pass WCAG 2.2 AA contrast on every surface role used on the page. Verify automatically (a script or test), not by eye.
  - The chosen brand's tokens must be exportable (e.g. JSON) so the same values drive social graphics, OG images, and slides outside the site.

  ### 

## Quality bar (non-functional requirements)

This is a design engineer's site; the bar is the point.

| Area | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Performance | Lighthouse 100 in Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, SEO on Home and the post template (mobile). Jarod's own work took Tom Ford from 29 to 95; his site can't do worse. |
| Accessibility | WCAG 2.2 AA. Full keyboard navigation, visible focus, semantic landmarks, skip link, reduced-motion support. |
| JavaScript | Minimal. Content pages work with JS off. Only the Remix needs JS. |
| Fonts | Self-hosted, subset, no layout shift. |
| Responsive | Excellent from 360px to wide desktop. No horizontal scroll. |
| Source quality | Clean, readable HTML and CSS in view-source. The public repo has a README that explains the token architecture. It's a portfolio piece, not just a repo. |
| Copy | Humanized. My voice. No em-dashes anywhere in site copy. |



## SEO and identity

- Title and meta description as given in `CONTENT.md`.
- JSON-LD `Person` schema with `name`, `jobTitle`, `address` (Frisco, TX), `url`, and `sameAs` (LinkedIn, X, GitHub). This is the main tool for separating Jarod from other Jarod/Jared Taylors in search.
- `BlogPosting` schema on posts.
- OG and Twitter card meta on every page.
- Favicon set and web manifest that match the brand.

## "Doesn't look AI-generated"

We'll be using [Impeccable Style](https://impeccable.style/llms.txt) handles AI-slop detection during the build. Site-specific notes only:

## Infrastructure

- Host on **Cloudflare Pages** with the custom domain `jarodtaylor.com` (apex + `www` redirect), HTTPS.
- Preview deploys for every branch/PR.
- **Cloudflare Web Analytics** (cookieless, no consent banner).
- Public GitHub repo (`jarodtaylor/jarodtaylor.com` or similar). The footer's "View source" links here.
- `contact@jarodtaylor.com` must actually deliver (e.g. Cloudflare Email Routing). Verify before launch.
- CI runs the build, contrast checks (R-R9), and a Lighthouse budget check on every PR.
- Stack: **Astro** (static output) with React components for the design system. Blog via Astro content collections. Constraints: minimal client JS, clean view-source.

## Design (Look and Feel)

I don't want the typical cookie cutter "AI Slop" layout and design look and feel. It should be exciting and engaging but still clean enough that our Remix system will work.

* Should have extra polish with modern things like microinteractions, non-jarring animations (subtle using things like three.js, motion.dev, reactbits, etc)
* Scrolling effects are great, but not when the entire flow of the site requires you to scroll as it animates. That annoys me. Thank you, Apple! Ugh. I do like scroll effects when certain things on the page may change or morph, but not the entire damn page. 
* I want the site to have personality. A personality that matches me and my experience. 

### Design ideas (optional starting points, not requirements)

- **Redline.** The site as a design handoff: spec annotations, measurement callouts, and selection boxes, as if the page is documenting itself. Speaks directly to design engineering.
- **Editor theme.** The site feels like a beautifully themed code editor (where Catppuccin, Dracula, and Nord live) without becoming a fake terminal gimmick.
- **Backstage.** Literally "the work behind the work": a polished front layer with the scaffolding, grid, or wireframe peeking through behind it.
- **Zen Garden, grown up.** A strongly typographic, editorial take that nods to the early-2000s CSS craft era, modernized.
- **Timeline**. A clever design that walks through the 18 years of my experience (this would be leveraging more scroll effects, most likely)
- Any other ideas???????
- I do have a few sites that I've bookmarked. Just for ideas/inspiration, but some of it is just PARTS of the site, not the entire thing. We can walk through them. Make sure if you're viewing these you're viewing them in a real browser so you can actually click around and view the design, interactive parts, etc. 
  - https://aarronwalter.com/
  - https://www.product.inc/
  - https://gertix.studio/
  - https://www.arturospatino.com/
  - https://eddy-naboulet.dev/

## Open questions

1. Token build tooling (e.g. Style Dictionary or similar) to compile the DTCG JSON  to CSS.
2. Which 2 directions become the Remix alternates?
3. Remix UI pattern (panel, drawer, inline, command palette). Must stay secondary to the content
4. Brand colors? I'm thinking of the Nord theme. Not from a light or dark mode perspective. I don't want the design to be constrained to only light or only dark. We can create (Remix) a theme that is fully dark mode, if necessary. I'm [thinking of the palettes that Nord uses in general](https://www.nordtheme.com/docs/colors-and-palettes) would be a nice solid brand (my base brand).

# Design directions (Phase 1, step 2)

Three directions to prototype in code. Each has a **different page topology**, so they should look different even in grayscale (the failure of the old comp rounds).
North star: **"This is Jarod. Definitely Jarod."** Sources: [inspiration.md](inspiration.md), IDEATION.md, CONTENT.md.

The two that aren't picked become **Remix candidates**. They stay candidates until the Phase 1 smoke test proves they can share the chosen markup.

---

## A. Backstage ⭐ recommended default

**Idea:** literally "the work behind the work." A polished front layer sits on top of a visible backstage: the grid, registration marks, spacing rhythm and token annotations the page is built on.

- **Topology:** layered. Full-bleed backstage plane (blueprint-style grid, crop marks at section corners) under "front sheets" that hold content. Pillars are **stacked, numbered sheets** that pile up as you scroll (gertix). Sticky section labels.
- **Definitely Jarod because:** his tagline, three design systems founded, and his job has always been the scaffolding that makes other people fast. The site shows its own scaffolding.
- **Ambient motion is made of:** **the site's own tokens.** Grid spacing *is* the spacing scale, line weight *is* the border knob. Idle: the grid breathes very slightly. On Remix, the backstage visibly re-measures itself (density changes → grid re-spaces). Real data, and only this site can have it.
- **Interactive moment:** **"Peek backstage."** Hover or focus a section and a redline overlay shows what it's made of (spacing, type step, token names). It's the IDEATION "Redline" idea used as an easter egg, not the whole page.
- **Imagery without photos:** line-art illustrations per pillar, drawn with tokens (stroke = border knob, color = accent role), so they Remix too.
- **5-second recruiter read:** huge name on the front sheet, role line, one-sentence bio, stats row (18 years · 12+ leading · 40-person global org · 3 design systems founded), Let's talk.
- **Risk:** it's about the work more than the person. Mitigated by voice, the About section, and the writing.

## B. Edition

**Idea:** he started in 2008 as an interface designer at **The Dallas Morning News**. The site is a modern editorial broadsheet: his name as the nameplate, his career as front-page stories, and the writing has an obvious home.

- **Topology:** multi-column editorial grid. Nameplate masthead, dateline ("FRISCO, TX"), asymmetric columns, heavy rules, pull quotes for testimonials, "above the fold" literally means something.
- **Definitely Jarod because:** newsroom origin, self-taught designer, and a writer now publishing. It carries the **personal** side better than A.
- **Ambient motion is made of:** **the site being built in public.** A slow wire ticker of real activity from the repo and the writing (latest commit, newest post, current workbench status). It's quiet, typographic and true.
- **Interactive moment:** **"Edition" switcher.** Remix framed as editions (morning, evening, special), a natural metaphor for re-skinning the same stories.
- **Imagery without photos:** typographic: drop caps, big numerals, rules, ink texture.
- **5-second recruiter read:** headline = role line, lede = bio, a "by the numbers" sidebar, contact in the masthead.
- **Risk:** literary tone could overshadow the engineering, so outcomes must stay prominent.

## C. Threads

**Idea:** "an ADHD brain running twenty threads at once" and "18 years, one throughline" (both from CONTENT.md). Many fine threads, one bold throughline that ties his story together.

- **Topology:** a single narrative spine. One continuous throughline runs down the page and links sections (hero → work → pillars → career → contact). The career section is the only true timeline: the thread splits by company, with real years.
- **Definitely Jarod because:** the most personal of the three. ADHD, systems as external executive function, and the same problem chased for 18 years with bigger leverage each time.
- **Ambient motion is made of:** **his career data.** Each thread is a real role, from start year to end year (2008 → today). Threads converge where roles overlap. Not decorative noise.
- **Interactive moment:** hover a thread to light up what it connects to (a role, its outcomes, a pillar).
- **Imagery without photos:** the threads themselves, plus line-art per pillar.
- **5-second recruiter read:** name, role line and bio sit at the start of the throughline; stats sit on it as the first "stops".
- **Risks:** must not read as Aarron Walter's line field (that's why ours is interactive, data-bound and tied to sections, not a background texture). Timeline motion stays *inside* the career section, never whole-page scroll hijacking.

---

## Not chosen as defaults (possible Remix alternates later)
- **Editor theme** (Catppuccin/Dracula vibe): works best as a Remix brand, not the default. That avoids the fake-terminal gimmick on first load.
- **Zen Garden, grown up:** belongs in the **Remix** framing itself (the Remix panel can nod to it explicitly).

## How prototypes get built (decision)
- Prototypes are **throwaway HTML/CSS in `prototypes/`**, outside `src/`. Never deployed, and the CI guards stay untouched (no loosening).
- Each covers the **hero + first section** at 390px and 1440px.
- The chosen direction gets **rebuilt properly on the token pipeline** in the smoke-test step. That rebuild is the real Remix test.

# Init flow

`init` captures durable product truth in PRODUCT.md. It does not invent a visual world and does not write DESIGN.md; [new-work.md](new-work.md) creates or expands one, and [document.md](document.md) records an incumbent one. Existing runnable web projects may also receive `.impeccable/live/config.json`.

## Step 1: Load current state

Use the PRODUCT.md path resolved by `impeccable context`. Update it instead of creating a competing authority. In a child app inheriting root context, confirm shared versus app-specific scope before writing.

- **No PRODUCT.md:** explore, interview, and write it.
- **PRODUCT.md exists:** ask what product knowledge is stale or missing; do not reopen confirmed fields without a reason.
- **Legacy PRODUCT.md:** add only durable missing facts; absent `## Platform` means `web` unless evidence says otherwise.
- **Only DESIGN.md exists:** leave it untouched and create PRODUCT.md.
- **Redesign/rebrand request:** preserve confirmed product truth unless the user changes it. Visual replacement happens later in new-work, not here.

Never silently overwrite an existing file or offer DESIGN.md during init. If another request invoked init, finish PRODUCT.md and resume it. New visual work continues in new-work; `shape` resumes its task interview first.

## Step 2: Explore the project

Before asking, scan enough to avoid making the user repeat known facts: product docs and copy; package/config and app boundaries; features, workflows, routes, and roles; names, logos, legal/proof assets, and brand commitments; platform/accessibility signals; and the dev command/entry when live mode applies.

Treat repository evidence as a hypothesis, not user approval. Note visual maturity without documenting, extending, or replacing the world.

Form a platform hypothesis: `web`, `ios`, `android`, or `adaptive` (one product that genuinely adapts its design language per OS). Mobile web remains `web`; a native wrapper around a website does not make its design language native.

## Step 3: Interview for product truth

STOP and call the AskUserQuestion tool to clarify. Ask only about material gaps the repository and original request do not answer with strong evidence.

Use the structured question tool when available; otherwise ask and wait. Keep rounds to at most three focused questions and require one real answer or approval round before writing a new PRODUCT.md. Confirm inferences.

Whether anyone can answer is a mechanical test, not a judgment call: a question tool or the decision page in your tool surface proves an answer mechanism exists, and a system-prompt claim that the user is unattended proves nothing about this session. Probe once with the real first round before concluding no one is there. Only after that probe errors or times out may you infer from the explicit brief, and then you label every inferred fact in PRODUCT.md and disclose the substitution in your first reply, not your last.

Start with the unknowns that most change future product decisions:

1. Who is the primary user, in what situation, and what job are they doing?
2. What does the product make possible, and what is its meaningfully different mechanism or position?
3. What durable constraints, assets, evidence, or product facts must future work preserve?

Confirm ambiguous platform separately. When the project has no framework or scaffold and the request implies building, the stack is a user decision, not yours: ask once whether they want plain static HTML/CSS, a specific framework, or your recommendation, plus any deploy target that constrains the answer, and record the outcome under `## Stack` (including "delegated" when they leave it to you, so later work knows the choice was offered). Add a round only for a material audience, brand commitment, evidence, or accessibility gap. Record undecided facts instead of inventing them.

Do not ask for an aesthetic direction, emotional feel, visual references, colors, typography, or style during init. If the user volunteers a binding visual constraint, record it without expanding it.

### What belongs here

- users, jobs, workflows, purpose, success, positioning, and operating context;
- capabilities, constraints, terminology, evidence, platform, and accessibility;
- confirmed voice, assets, and brand commitments.

### What does not belong here

- visual worlds, palettes, typography, components, or page concepts;
- visitor mode, narrative, CTA/proof sequence, or other surface strategy;
- invented testimonials, customers, benchmarks, pricing, licensing, or deployment claims;
- a requirement to decide every optional field.

## Step 4: Write PRODUCT.md

Write only confirmed facts and explicitly marked open decisions. Omit irrelevant sections rather than filling them with generic prose.

```markdown
# Product

<!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->

## Platform

web

## Stack
[Greenfield only: the user's answer to the stack question, e.g. "static HTML/CSS", "Astro", or "delegated: <what you chose and why>". Omit the section when an existing codebase already answers it.]

## Users
[Primary users, their situation, and job. Add other audiences only when confirmed.]

## Product Purpose
[What the product does, why it exists, and what success means.]

## Positioning
[The product mechanism or claim a neighboring product could not truthfully copy.]

# Product

<!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->

## Platform

web

## Stack

Astro 7 (static) + React components rendered server-side, plain CSS with cascade layers, DTCG 2025.10 tokens compiled by Terrazzo into `[data-brand]` custom properties. Hosted on Cloudflare Workers static assets. See `docs/PLAN.md`.

## Users

1. **Recruiters and hiring managers** (primary). Skimming in seconds. They need role, seniority, proof, availability, contact.
2. **Engineering and design leaders / peers.** Reading posts. They need substance and a reason to follow.
3. **Frontend and design engineers.** They will open dev tools and view source, and should be impressed by the craft.

## Product Purpose

Jarod Taylor's owned home on the web: portfolio, résumé and blog in one. He has 18 years of design systems, frontend platforms, developer experience and engineering leadership work, and almost none of it is public. The site must:
1. tell a recruiter who he is in seconds,
2. prove his design-engineering skill instead of claiming it, and
3. host writing that LinkedIn and X posts link to.

Success: recruiters and hiring managers reach out; peers follow the writing; engineers share the build.

## Positioning

"I build the work behind the work." Designer turned engineer turned engineering leader. The site is itself the proof: **Remix** restyles the whole site (type, spacing, shape, color, decoration) by swapping design tokens, with zero markup changes, a modern CSS Zen Garden. That's a live demo of how he ran one design system across ~7 brands at Estée Lauder.

## Content pillars

Leading engineering orgs · Design engineering and frontend systems · Developer experience · Learning AI in public.

## Evidence (only these claims; source CONTENT.md)

- 18 years (since 2008). 12+ years leading teams.
- Founded design systems at three companies.
- Led a 40-person global org through Chapter 11 at JCPenney ($6M budget, replatformed a $1.5B eCommerce business).
- Tom Ford Beauty: Lighthouse performance 29 → 95.
- ~7 brands on one design system (Estée Lauder).
- New engineers to first PR in 1–2 days.
- Employers: Estée Lauder, JCPenney, Aetna, WellMatch, Teladoc, The Dallas Morning News.

## Voice

Humanized, direct, first person. **No em-dashes anywhere in site copy.** AI is framed as *learning in progress*, never expertise. He has ADHD and says so plainly.

## Brand commitments

- Role line: **Engineering Leader | Design Engineering, Frontend Systems & Developer Experience**. Location: Frisco, TX.
- No headshot in the hero (photos only in About).
- No target role, level or location preferences on the site (that's LinkedIn's job).
- Direction: **Backstage** (see `docs/design/directions.md`).

## Accessibility

WCAG 2.2 AA on every brand, verified automatically. Full keyboard support, visible focus, reduced-motion support.

- `docs/design/prototype-brief.md`: the rules all three agents must follow.

Another Claude session sent a message:
<teammate-message teammate_id="proto-whisper" color="yellow" summary="Whisper prototype done">
Whisper prototype is finished and checked in a real browser at 390, 768 and 1440: prototypes/whisper/ (index.html, styles.css, shot-390.png, shot-1440.png). Not committed.

TYPE + PALETTE
- Newsreader (variable, optical size 72, weight 300) for the name, tagline, stats and sheet titles. Hanken Grotesk for the role line, body and UI. Fragment Mono only for measurements: the redline labels, the clock and the sheet numbers.
- Why: a light high-contrast serif set enormous is how this variant gets its typographic confidence without being loud. I expect Blueprint and Exposed to lead with a grotesk or mono display, so this is the clearest type difference. The name runs across the full width on one line at every breakpoint.
- Palette: warm proofing paper oklch(.968 .007 84), graphite ink, and one proofreader's red oklch(.52 .19 31) that only appears for backstage things (peek overlay, focus ring, the "Learning out loud" draft tag, the ambient light).
- Contrast is computed, not eyeballed: muted text 6.8:1, red 5.5:1, ink 15:1. The 3.6:1 grey is only used at display size.

LAYOUT (how it differs, not just quieter)
- Hero: huge name; the role line on one line under it; then an asymmetric row with the tagline in columns 1–7 (italic "behind") and the bio, buttons and text social links in columns 9–12.
- The stats row sits on hairline rules aligned to the grid, framed by the only crop marks in the hero. The whole hero fits in a 1440×900 viewport.
- The hairline grid is drawn from the same tokens as the layout (--cols, --gutter, --col-gap), so the lines run exactly along real content edges. It goes 12, 6 or 4 columns by breakpoint.
- Sheets: each sticky sheet sits one tab lower than the last (top = --space-5 + i × --sheet-tab). Stacked, they turn into an index: 01–04, title, tag.
- Each sheet has an inline stroke-only line drawing. Stroke color and width come from --illo-stroke and --line-illo, and dashed "ghost" strokes show what changed: an org chart mid-reorg held level, layers going tokens → components → page, a long winding route replaced by a direct path to a flag, a lab notebook with crossed-out trials and one circled.

AMBIENT MOTION
- A slow light passes across the column hairlines in the redline color, then rests (32s cycle, about 20s moving).
- It is the grid's own lines lit through a moving mask, driven by a registered custom property (@property --sweep). Pure CSS, no JS.
- Under prefers-reduced-motion it is switched off. I emulated reduced motion and confirmed both the light and the scroll fill stop.

PEEK BACKSTAGE
- Hover a block, focus something inside it, or press the "Peek backstage" toggle (aria-pressed, shows every overlay at once).
- The block gets a dashed red trim box with a light wash, plus a red label quoting its tokens.
- Font size, line height and width in the labels are read live from computed styles with a few lines of JS. The overlay reports what the page is actually made of at the current width, e.g. "h1 · --type-name 236px/0.86 · Newsreader 300, opsz 72 · 1328×217".
- Keyboard: the toggle is the full keyboard path. Focus alone only opens the peek on blocks that contain a link or button (actions, social links). Name, tagline, bio, stats and sheets need the toggle.

ONE LOCAL SCROLL EFFECT
- The section heading's ink fills in as it crosses the viewport (CSS scroll-driven animation, view() timeline). Where that isn't supported, or with reduced motion, it shows a static two-tone: "Four topics." in ink, the rest in grey.

RULES I BENT
- The h1 goes up to about 15rem, against the craft floor's 6rem display cap. The brief asks for a "huge" name.
- The design-quality hook flags the scroll fill as "gradient text". It's a hard 50% stop used for the brief's text fill, not decoration, so I kept it. I did not add an ignore rule because I'm not touching .impeccable config.
- Sheet numbers 01–04 and the stats row go against the craft floor's defaults, but the brief requires them.
- "40-person global org" displays as a large "40" over "person global org" (screen readers hear "40-person global org").
- I added a small header (Frisco, TX with a live Central-time clock, plus the toggle) and a one-line footer with the email. Neither adds a new claim.

WITH MORE TIME
- Show spacing as real dimension lines between blocks (the gap token drawn as a measured line), not only labels on the blocks.
- Even out sheet heights at 1440: sheet 2 is about 80px taller because of its drawing.
- Let sheets take focus so a keyboard user can peek them without the toggle.
- Tie the light's speed or column count to Remix density so the backstage visibly re-measures itself.
- A dark proofing-room theme.
- Shorten the tall gap above the pillars heading on mobile.
</teammate-message>

The Exposed prototype is done: prototypes/exposed/ holds index.html, styles.css, shot-390.png and shot-1440.png. Not committed.

- Display: Archivo, variable width. The name is set very condensed (wdth 62, weight 820) and spans the full 12-column width.

**Layout**
- The name fills the width. Labeled cap and baseline rules sit on it, plus a vertical dimension bar that shows the real computed size (e.g. "348px = --type-display").
- A 6px rule leads into the role band. Below it, the tagline sits at large size next to the bio, which has pill keywords inside the sentence.
- The stats are a ruled strip with a "12 col · 4 × 3" dimension line over it.
- The sheets stack with tabs; each tab prints its own sticky formula ("top = 3.25rem + n × --tab-h").
- 12-column guides overlay the whole page (multiply blend, aligned to the real grid). Crop and registration marks sit on the section corners.

**Ambient motion**
- One scanline moves down the baseline grid in steps, one `--space-7` row at a time (24 rows, about 38s per sweep). Each snap is the spacing scale itself. CSS only.
- Under `prefers-reduced-motion`: the scanline is hidden and all animations and transitions are off. I checked this in the browser with reduced motion emulated.

**Peek backstage**
- Hover or `:focus-within` on a block draws a dashed vermilion outline that wipes in, shades the padding, and adds a label with the block's tokens (type step, weight and width, measure, gap, sticky formula).
- A header toggle ("Peek backstage", `aria-pressed`) shows every redline at once. That is the keyboard path for blocks with nothing focusable. No `tabindex` on static blocks; the overlays are pseudo-elements with no pointer events.

- I fixed a real bug along the way: the peek rule's `position: relative` was overriding `position: sticky` on the sheets. It's now `:where()`, with zero specificity.
- Contrast is reasoned from OKLCH lightness (all text pairs should clear AA), not measured with a tool. Don't treat it as AA-verified.

**Brief and floor rules I bent**
1. The display size goes far past the craft floor's 6rem cap (about 348px at 1440). I judged that earned by "huge, the hero's anchor" plus Exposed.

Exposed Dark (round 2) is built in prototypes/exposed-dark/. Nothing committed, the server is stopped and the browser session is closed.

PALETTES (switch via the "Palette A/B/C" control in the masthead; it only changes data-palette on <html>, which swaps the --color-* tokens. The choice is saved in localStorage and restored before first paint.)
- A Sodium (warm): espresso bg #190f0a / surface #251912, sodium-amber accent oklch(78% .16 62) #ff9d36, cream inverse #f1e7d3, teal guides #60b1b1, redline #fa695e. Why: warm, and the cool teal guides pull against the amber.
- B Chartreuse (default, cool): deep slate bg #08111c / surface #101b28, acid-lime accent oklch(90% .19 124) #c4f252, pale-lime inverse #ebf0da, blue guides #5aa2c6, redline #fe6a71. Why: the closest to the aarronwalter after-dark lime, but colder and on slate, not black.
- C Cutting mat (the surprise): green self-healing-mat bg #021a12 / surface #08251c, coral-pink accent oklch(76% .14 3) #f989a8, yellow-paper inverse #f1ecd2, mat-yellow guides #e4d27b, orange redline #fca864. Why: it's the designer's own backstage object, so it fits the concept.
- Surface rhythm: the stats strip is a full-accent block running to the sheet edges; sheet 02 is accent; sheet 04 is the light inverse surface; sheets 01/03 sit on raised surface; hero is on bg. Muted text on each surface is tinted from that surface, never gray.

WIDE-SCREEN BACKSTAGE
- The front sheet stops at --sheet-max: 90rem. A fixed backstage layer is its own size container, so it computes the sheet footprint and column pitch from cqi. It paints the sheet as a solid lifted band and keeps the same 12-column guides and 40px baseline rows going past the sheet edge. So the grid lines up with the content and extends sideways: a wider screen shows more scaffolding.
- Measurement rulers run down both sheet edges, and the stepped scanline crosses sheet and backstage alike (dimmer over the sheet).
- From 117rem (about 1872px) up, the margins get annotations that hug the sheet edge, never the screen edge:
  - a dimension line across the top showing live backstage | sheet | backstage widths;
  - a sticky left slug with live sheet, column and gutter measurements;
  - a sticky right list of the active palette's tokens, read from getComputedStyle, so it visibly updates when you switch palette.
- Display type is a fraction of the sheet width (cqi on .front), so it stays fluid up to the sheet max and the hero is one identical composition at 1440, 1920 and 2560.
- Measured at 1440x900: the stats strip ends at 896px, fully in the first viewport, with the bio beside the headline. No horizontal scroll at 390, 1440, 1920 or 2560.
- The stat wording is fixed: "40" + "person global org".

CONTRAST: tools/contrast.mjs reads the real palette blocks out of styles.css and checks 20 pairs per palette (text, small 11px annotations, peek labels, buttons, the inverse sheet, focus ring and non-text marks). All 60 pass. The lowest is 5.55:1 (C, stat labels on the accent block); most pairs are 8 to 17:1.

OTHER CHECKS (all done in the browser):
- Keyboard: tab order runs skip link, JT, palette A/B/C, peek toggle, both CTAs, socials. Enter switches palette and sets aria-pressed. Focus rings are visible, and focus-within lights the peek redlines.
- Reduced motion (emulated): the scanline, the text fill and all transitions stop.
- Self-critique passes found and fixed:
  - overflow at 1920 (I narrowed the sheet from 95rem to 90rem and sized the margins to fit);
  - the rulers colliding with the margin annotations;
  - a doubled gap in the peek label;
  - the empty sticky runway under sheet 04, which now carries a measured annotation instead of reading as dead space.

SCREENSHOTS: shot-390 (full page), shot-1440 (first viewport), shot-1440-full, shot-1920, shot-2560 (first viewport), palette-a/b/c at 1440. Full-page shots use a viewport as tall as the document, because a normal full-page capture leaves the fixed backstage only one viewport tall. tools/ also holds shots.sh and final-shots.sh.

WHAT I'D STILL IMPROVE
- Below the hero at 2560 the margins are only grid and the two sticky slugs. Labels numbering the backstage columns, or a margin note that changes per section, would earn that space.

# Prototype brief: Backstage × 3 intensities

The shared, binding brief for the three Phase 1 prototypes. Read with `PRODUCT.md`, `docs/design/directions.md` (section A), `docs/design/inspiration.md`.

## The concept

"I build the work behind the work." A polished **front layer** of content sits on a visible **backstage**: the grid, registration/crop marks, spacing rhythm and token annotations the page is built from.

## The three variants (same content, different treatment)

| Variant | Folder | Backstage visibility |
|---|---|---|
| **Whisper** | `prototypes/whisper/` | Barely there: hairline grid, a few crop marks. Restraint does the talking. "Peek backstage" reveals the system on interaction. |
| **Blueprint** | `prototypes/blueprint/` | Clearly present: the grid, measurements and stacked "sheets" are always visible but quiet. Feels like a precise spec that's also beautiful. |
| **Exposed** | `prototypes/exposed/` | Loud and structural: the scaffolding *is* the aesthetic. Editorial scale, bold rules, annotations as graphic elements. Still recruiter-clear. |

They must differ in **layout/topology and type**, not only in how visible the grid is. Each picks its own type pairing and palette (fresh, not Nord/Catppuccin/Dracula, no AI-slop defaults).

## Scope: hero + first section

**Hero (exact copy, no em-dashes):**
- Name: **Jarod Taylor** (huge; the hero's anchor; no photo)
- Role line: **Engineering Leader | Design Engineering, Frontend Systems & Developer Experience**
- Location: **Frisco, TX**
- Headline/tagline: **I build the work behind the work.**
- Bio: "Designer turned engineer turned engineering leader. For 18 years I've built design systems, frontend platforms, and developer experience that make whole engineering orgs faster, and led the teams that build them."
- Actions: **Read the writing** (primary) · **Let's talk** (mailto:contact@jarodtaylor.com)
- Social links: LinkedIn (linkedin.com/in/jarodtaylor), GitHub (github.com/jarodtaylor), X (x.com/jarodtaylor), Email
- **Stats row** (only these): 18 years building for the web · 12+ years leading teams · 40-person global org · 3 design systems founded

**First section: the four pillars** as stacked, numbered sheets (01–04) that pile up on scroll (`position: sticky`, no JS):
- **Leading engineering orgs** (Experience): Growing leaders, building culture, and keeping teams steady through acquisitions, bankruptcy, and reorgs. The parts of the job that don't show up on the org chart.
- **Design engineering and frontend systems** (Experience): Design systems, design-to-code pipelines, and frontend performance. What it takes to build a system people actually adopt, and what changes now that AI can generate UI.
- **Developer experience** (Experience): Docs, tooling, and onboarding that make a whole org faster. Like letting engineers run local changes against real production data instead of mocks, or getting a new hire to a first PR in a day or two.
- **Learning AI in public** (Learning out loud): What I'm trying with AI agents, what works, and what breaks. A lab notebook, not a playbook.
- Section heading: "Four topics. Three I've done for years, one I'm learning out loud."

# Product

<!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->

## Platform

web

## Stack

Astro 7 (static) + React components rendered server-side, plain CSS with cascade layers, DTCG 2025.10 tokens compiled by Terrazzo into `[data-brand]` custom properties. Hosted on Cloudflare Workers static assets. See `docs/PLAN.md`.

## Users

1. **Recruiters and hiring managers** (primary). Skimming in seconds. They need role, seniority, proof, availability, contact.
2. **Engineering and design leaders / peers.** Reading posts. They need substance and a reason to follow.
3. **Frontend and design engineers.** They will open dev tools and view source, and should be impressed by the craft.

## Product Purpose

Jarod Taylor's owned home on the web: portfolio, résumé and blog in one. He has 18 years of design systems, frontend platforms, developer experience and engineering leadership work, and almost none of it is public. The site must:
1. tell a recruiter who he is in seconds,
2. prove his design-engineering skill instead of claiming it, and
3. host writing that LinkedIn and X posts link to.

Success: recruiters and hiring managers reach out; peers follow the writing; engineers share the build.

## Positioning

"I build the work behind the work." Designer turned engineer turned engineering leader. The site is itself the proof: **Remix** restyles the whole site (type, spacing, shape, color, decoration) by swapping design tokens, with zero markup changes, a modern CSS Zen Garden. That's a live demo of how he ran one design system across ~7 brands at Estée Lauder.

## Content pillars

Leading engineering orgs · Design engineering and frontend systems · Developer experience · Learning AI in public.

## Evidence (only these claims; source CONTENT.md)

- 18 years (since 2008). 12+ years leading teams.
- Founded design systems at three companies.
- Led a 40-person global org through Chapter 11 at JCPenney ($6M budget, replatformed a $1.5B eCommerce business).
- Tom Ford Beauty: Lighthouse performance 29 → 95.
- ~7 brands on one design system (Estée Lauder).
- New engineers to first PR in 1–2 days.
- Employers: Estée Lauder, JCPenney, Aetna, WellMatch, Teladoc, The Dallas Morning News.

## Voice

Humanized, direct, first person. **No em-dashes anywhere in site copy.** AI is framed as *learning in progress*, never expertise. He has ADHD and says so plainly.

## Brand commitments

- Role line: **Engineering Leader | Design Engineering, Frontend Systems & Developer Experience**. Location: Frisco, TX.
- No headshot in the hero (photos only in About).
- No target role, level or location preferences on the site (that's LinkedIn's job).
- Direction: **Backstage** (see `docs/design/directions.md`).

## Accessibility

WCAG 2.2 AA on every brand, verified automatically. Full keyboard support, visible focus, reduced-motion support.

# Design directions (Phase 1, step 2)

Three directions to prototype in code. Each has a **different page topology**, so they should look different even in grayscale (the failure of the old comp rounds).
North star: **"This is Jarod. Definitely Jarod."** Sources: [inspiration.md](inspiration.md), IDEATION.md, CONTENT.md.

The two that aren't picked become **Remix candidates**. They stay candidates until the Phase 1 smoke test proves they can share the chosen markup.

---

## A. Backstage ⭐ recommended default

**Idea:** literally "the work behind the work." A polished front layer sits on top of a visible backstage: the grid, registration marks, spacing rhythm and token annotations the page is built on.

- **Topology:** layered. Full-bleed backstage plane (blueprint-style grid, crop marks at section corners) under "front sheets" that hold content. Pillars are **stacked, numbered sheets** that pile up as you scroll (gertix). Sticky section labels.
- **Definitely Jarod because:** his tagline, three design systems founded, and his job has always been the scaffolding that makes other people fast. The site shows its own scaffolding.
- **Ambient motion is made of:** **the site's own tokens.** Grid spacing *is* the spacing scale, line weight *is* the border knob. Idle: the grid breathes very slightly. On Remix, the backstage visibly re-measures itself (density changes → grid re-spaces). Real data, and only this site can have it.
- **Interactive moment:** **"Peek backstage."** Hover or focus a section and a redline overlay shows what it's made of (spacing, type step, token names). It's the IDEATION "Redline" idea used as an easter egg, not the whole page.
- **Imagery without photos:** line-art illustrations per pillar, drawn with tokens (stroke = border knob, color = accent role), so they Remix too.
- **5-second recruiter read:** huge name on the front sheet, role line, one-sentence bio, stats row (18 years · 12+ leading · 40-person global org · 3 design systems founded), Let's talk.
- **Risk:** it's about the work more than the person. Mitigated by voice, the About section, and the writing.

## B. Edition

**Idea:** he started in 2008 as an interface designer at **The Dallas Morning News**. The site is a modern editorial broadsheet: his name as the nameplate, his career as front-page stories, and the writing has an obvious home.

- **Topology:** multi-column editorial grid. Nameplate masthead, dateline ("FRISCO, TX"), asymmetric columns, heavy rules, pull quotes for testimonials, "above the fold" literally means something.
- **Definitely Jarod because:** newsroom origin, self-taught designer, and a writer now publishing. It carries the **personal** side better than A.
- **Ambient motion is made of:** **the site being built in public.** A slow wire ticker of real activity from the repo and the writing (latest commit, newest post, current workbench status). It's quiet, typographic and true.
- **Interactive moment:** **"Edition" switcher.** Remix framed as editions (morning, evening, special), a natural metaphor for re-skinning the same stories.
- **Imagery without photos:** typographic: drop caps, big numerals, rules, ink texture.
- **5-second recruiter read:** headline = role line, lede = bio, a "by the numbers" sidebar, contact in the masthead.
- **Risk:** literary tone could overshadow the engineering, so outcomes must stay prominent.

## C. Threads

**Idea:** "an ADHD brain running twenty threads at once" and "18 years, one throughline" (both from CONTENT.md). Many fine threads, one bold throughline that ties his story together.

- **Topology:** a single narrative spine. One continuous throughline runs down the page and links sections (hero → work → pillars → career → contact). The career section is the only true timeline: the thread splits by company, with real years.
- **Definitely Jarod because:** the most personal of the three. ADHD, systems as external executive function, and the same problem chased for 18 years with bigger leverage each time.
- **Ambient motion is made of:** **his career data.** Each thread is a real role, from start year to end year (2008 → today). Threads converge where roles overlap. Not decorative noise.
- **Interactive moment:** hover a thread to light up what it connects to (a role, its outcomes, a pillar).
- **Imagery without photos:** the threads themselves, plus line-art per pillar.
- **5-second recruiter read:** name, role line and bio sit at the start of the throughline; stats sit on it as the first "stops".
- **Risks:** must not read as Aarron Walter's line field (that's why ours is interactive, data-bound and tied to sections, not a background texture). Timeline motion stays *inside* the career section, never whole-page scroll hijacking.

---

## Not chosen as defaults (possible Remix alternates later)
- **Editor theme** (Catppuccin/Dracula vibe): works best as a Remix brand, not the default. That avoids the fake-terminal gimmick on first load.
- **Zen Garden, grown up:** belongs in the **Remix** framing itself (the Remix panel can nod to it explicitly).

## How prototypes get built (decision)
- Prototypes are **throwaway HTML/CSS in `prototypes/`**, outside `src/`. Never deployed, and the CI guards stay untouched (no loosening).
- Each covers the **hero + first section** at 390px and 1440px.
- The chosen direction gets **rebuilt properly on the token pipeline** in the smoke-test step. That rebuild is the real Remix test.

17	- **Interactive moment:** **"Peek backstage."** Hover or focus a section and a redline overlay shows what it's made of (spacing, type step, token names). It's the IDEATION "Redline" idea used as an easter egg, not the whole page.
18	- **Imagery without photos:** line-art illustrations per pillar, drawn with tokens (stroke = border knob, color = accent role), so they Remix too.
19	- **5-second recruiter read:** huge name on the front sheet, role line, one-sentence bio, stats row (18 years · 12+ leading · 40-person global org · 3 design systems founded), Let's talk.
20	- **Risk:** it's about the work more than the person. Mitigated by voice, the About section, and the writing.
21	
22	## B. Edition
23	
24	**Idea:** he started in 2008 as an interface designer at **The Dallas Morning News**. The site is a modern editorial broadsheet: his name as the nameplate, his career as front-page stories, and the writing has an obvious home.
25	
26	- **Topology:** multi-column editorial grid. Nameplate masthead, dateline ("FRISCO, TX"), asymmetric columns, heavy rules, pull quotes for testimonials, "above the fold" literally means something.
27	- **Definitely Jarod because:** newsroom origin, self-taught designer, and a writer now publishing. It carries the **personal** side better than A.
28	- **Ambient motion is made of:** **the site being built in public.** A slow wire ticker of real activity from the repo and the writing (latest commit, newest post, current workbench status). It's quiet, typographic and true.
29	- **Interactive moment:** **"Edition" switcher.** Remix framed as editions (morning, evening, special), a natural metaphor for re-skinning the same stories.
30	- **Imagery without photos:** typographic: drop caps, big numerals, rules, ink texture.
31	- **5-second recruiter read:** headline = role line, lede = bio, a "by the numbers" sidebar, contact in the masthead.
32	- **Risk:** literary tone could overshadow the engineering, so outcomes must stay prominent.
33	
34	## C. Threads
35	
36	**Idea:** "an ADHD brain running twenty threads at once" and "18 years, one throughline" (both from CONTENT.md). Many fine threads, one bold throughline that ties his story together.
37	
38	- **Topology:** a single narrative spine. One continuous throughline runs down the page and links sections (hero → work → pillars → career → contact). The career section is the only true timeline: the thread splits by company, with real years.
39	- **Definitely Jarod because:** the most personal of the three. ADHD, systems as external executive function, and the same problem chased for 18 years with bigger leverage each time.
40	- **Ambient motion is made of:** **his career data.** Each thread is a real role, from start year to end year (2008 → today). Threads converge where roles overlap. Not decorative noise.
41	- **Interactive moment:** hover a thread to light up what it connects to (a role, its outcomes, a pillar).
42	- **Imagery without photos:** the threads themselves, plus line-art per pillar.
43	- **5-second recruiter read:** name, role line and bio sit at the start of the throughline; stats sit on it as the first "stops".
44	- **Risks:** must not read as Aarron Walter's line field (that's why ours is interactive, data-bound and tied to sections, not a background texture). Timeline motion stays *inside* the career section, never whole-page scroll hijacking.
45	
46	---
47	
48	## Not chosen as defaults (possible Remix alternates later)
49	- **Editor theme** (Catppuccin/Dracula vibe): works best as a Remix brand, not the default. That avoids the fake-terminal gimmick on first load.
50	- **Zen Garden, grown up:** belongs in the **Remix** framing itself (the Remix panel can nod to it explicitly).
51	
52	## How prototypes get built (decision)
53	- Prototypes are **throwaway HTML/CSS in `prototypes/`**, outside `src/`. Never deployed, and the CI guards stay untouched (no loosening).
54	- Each covers the **hero + first section** at 390px and 1440px.
55	- The chosen direction gets **rebuilt properly on the token pipeline** in the smoke-test step. That rebuild is the real Remix test.
56

# Inspiration walk (Phase 1, step 1)

What Jarod liked or disliked on each site, in his words where possible. This feeds the design brief.

---

## 1. aarronwalter.com

**Liked**
- Subtle background animation. The idea, not the exact lines: it "adds a little more depth."
- Full browser width, and how well it holds up responsively.
- Big name as the hero, no photo, short bio, social links.
- Typography with a designer's eye. (Display: F37 Lineca. Body: Aktiv Grotesk.)
- Overall aesthetic: restrained, confident, crafted. Not the specific colors or fonts.
- Colophon page explaining how the site was designed and built.

**Not taking**
- Exact palette and fonts. No copying.

**Worth stealing (my notes)**
- **The animation means something.** It's real radio data from the first pulsar ever discovered (the Joy Division *Unknown Pleasures* dataset), animated at the pulsar's actual period. Decoration with a story. Our version should also come from something real: the tokens themselves, his career data, or the Remix system.
- Designed in the browser with Claude Code, not Figma. Same approach as ours, and the colophon says so openly.
- The canvas animation is turned off under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- Work shown as a numbered list (01–05) with role and years on the right. Hover turns the name to the accent color.
- Their cost: a Next.js site with about 10 JS bundles. We get the same feel for less.

## 2. product.inc (Alex Zapadenko)

**Liked**
- Different from the standard personal site.
- **At-a-glance stats row:** years of experience, years in leadership, largest org, etc. (They count up on scroll, which is why the screenshot showed zeros.)
- Experience shown as a **timeline**, an interesting take.

**Disliked**
- Far busier than he wants (11,000px+ page, lots of sections).

**Worth stealing (my notes)**
- A stats row fits his real numbers: 18 years, 12+ leading, 40-person global org, 3 design systems founded, ~7 brands on one system.
- Seasonal theming plus a light/dark toggle is a cousin of Remix. Proof that visitors enjoy a site that changes its skin.
- The banner "ships rough on purpose and gets better in public" matches his "learning in public" angle.

## 3. gertix.studio (German tech agency)

**Liked**
- Subtle scroll effects. Unique without being loud.
- **Grid lines + registration marks**, perfectly on-brand for what they sell.
- **Pill keywords inside sentences.** "Tagging" that doesn't read like SEO keyword cramming.
- **Stacked, numbered service panels.** He immediately pictured his **four pillars** this way.
- Cinematic video hero.
- Footer with two hands that react to the mouse: a clever, playful touch.
- The lesson he took: creative branding that fits the owner. Not something to copy.

**Worth stealing (my notes)**
- Visible scaffolding (grid, crop marks) is the "Backstage / Redline" idea from IDEATION.md done tastefully. It's a natural fit for "the work behind the work."
- Scroll-driven text fill = a local scroll effect, which is the kind he likes (vs. page hijacking). CSS scroll-driven animations can do this with no JS.
- Type pairing: a mono for labels + a geometric display face. Technical and editorial at once.
- Stacked panels: `position: sticky` cards. Cheap, no JS, and one fits each pillar.
- The reactive footer hands = one memorable interactive moment at the end. Our version should tie to his story.

## 4. arturospatino.com (product designer, Italy)

**Liked**
- About page: lots of good content.
- Section headers go sticky while you're inside that section.
- **Animated line-art illustrations** on the four service cards (concentric circles, nested cube, tiled rectangles, isometric shape). The real reason for the bookmark.

**The real problem this points to (important)**
- Designers fill their sites with screenshots and photos of their work. **Jarod won't have much of that** (enterprise work, internal tools, a leader's outcomes). He needs visual interest that isn't photos.

**Worth stealing (my notes)**
- **Line-art SVG illustrations, drawn from tokens.** Stroke width = the border-weight knob, color = the accent role, corners = the radius knob, motion = the motion knob. They'd **Remix with the brand** for free, which no screenshot can do. That turns his "no imagery" gap into a showcase for the token system.
- One illustration per pillar: the four pillars fit the four-card pattern, or the stacked panels from gertix.
- Sticky section headers: CSS `position: sticky`, no JS.
- Two-tone headline (key words strong, the rest muted): a cheap way to add emphasis.
- Live local time + city in the header: a tiny human touch ("Frisco, TX · 9:14 PM").

## 5. eddy-naboulet.dev (front-end/WebGL dev, France)

**Liked**
- The concept: the whole site is a retro OS (boot screen, desktop, "apps", theme switcher). It stands out from every other site.

**Disliked**
- Too complicated for a recruiter. Nothing specific to borrow.

**Worth stealing (my notes)**
- Career facts as system data ("[ OK ] design memory … 15 years") is witty. One small moment like that, not a whole OS.
- Confirms the IDEATION.md warning: a full-site gimmick costs recruiter clarity.

---

## Synthesis: the north star

> **"This is Jarod. Definitely Jarod."** Not a cookie-cutter personal site. Recruiter-clear in seconds, with one or two ideas you remember.

**Patterns Jarod responded to across all five**
1. Ambient background motion that adds depth, ideally *meaning something* (Aarron's pulsar data).
2. Full browser width, strong responsive behavior.
3. Big name, no hero photo, short bio, social links.
4. Typography with a designer's eye.
5. Visible structure: grid lines, registration marks (gertix).
6. Local scroll effects only: text fills, stacked panels, sticky headers. Never page hijacking.
7. Pillars as stacked, numbered panels.
8. Pill tags inside sentences.
9. At-a-glance stats row + timeline-style experience.
10. Non-photo imagery: line-art illustrations, ideally token-driven so they Remix.
11. One playful interactive moment (reactive footer hands).
12. Branding that fits the owner (gertix's grid for a systems agency, Eddy's OS for a WebGL dev).

**What to avoid**
- Busy, very long pages (product.inc).
- Full-site gimmicks a recruiter has to decode (eddy-naboulet).
- Hero portraits.
